result.title: The Quiet Return of the Night Train
result.content:
At ten past nine in the evening the platform at the edge of the city is busier than it has been in years. Families with folded pushchairs, students with rucksacks and a man carrying a cello case all wait for the same long blue train, which will carry them through the night and set them down in another country before breakfast.

Sleeper services were cut back for decades, as cheap flights made the slow way seem old-fashioned. Now the operators say their carriages are full most nights of the week, and new routes are being added each season. Travellers say they like arriving rested, in the middle of a city, without the queues of an airport.

Why travellers are choosing it

Many of the passengers on the platform gave the same reasons: the time saved by sleeping through the journey, a smaller footprint than flying, and the simple pleasure of watching the lights of small towns pass the window. A retired teacher said she had not taken a night train since she was a girl, and wanted to see whether it was as she remembered.

Prices are higher than a budget flight booked well ahead, but lower than a flight and a hotel together, which is how several families on the platform said they had worked it out.

The operator publishes its timetable for anyone to use, and one passenger had worked out the journey's length on the platform with a few lines of code:

const departs = 21 * 60 + 10
const arrives = 7 * 60 + 45 + 24 * 60
console.log((arrives - departs) / 60)

What comes next

Two more routes are planned for next year, one of them crossing three borders in a single night. The operators are also ordering new carriages, with small rooms that have their own washbasins, and a dining car that serves breakfast as the train pulls into its last station.
